objectives.text: Identify major pharmacologic classes used in the management of endocrine conditions and describe their mechanisms of action.
Describe the indications, contraindications, adverse effects, and clinically significant interactions associated with medications used to treat endocrine conditions.
Compare pharmacologic agents within and across therapeutic classes to distinguish clinically relevant differences in efficacy, safety, and use.
Select appropriate pharmacologic therapy for common endocrine conditions based on clinical presentation and patient-specific factors.
Identify appropriate dosing, administration, and monitoring considerations for medications used in endocrine conditions.
Explain important medication-use and safety information to patients receiving pharmacotherapy for endocrine conditions.
Describe the hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis as a shared regulatory template, and identify where drug therapy intervenes at each level.
Identify the major agents used for growth hormone disorders, hyperprolactinemia, and disorders of antidiuretic hormone (diabetes insipidus, SIADH).
Describe the mechanisms, indications, and monitoring of thyroid hormone replacement and antithyroid drug therapy, including management of thyroid storm.
Compare glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid pharmacology, and identify agents used to block adrenocortical hormone synthesis or action.

Identify dosing, administration, and monitoring considerations, and explain key medication-safety counseling points to patients, including HPA-axis suppression and the need to taper chronic glucocorticoids.

about.text: **PA PHARMACOLOGY COURSE · LECTURE 4 · SESSION 1 OF 2** — Endocrine Pharmacotherapy. **Session 1: Pituitary, Thyroid, and Adrenal Pharmacology  |  Tuesday, November 10  |  8:30–11:00 AM**

One template runs this whole unit: hypothalamus drives the pituitary, the pituitary drives a target gland, and the gland’s hormone feeds back to turn the levels above it down. Every drug today replaces a hormone, blocks one, or interrupts that loop.

Arc: the shared HPA-template concept, then pituitary, thyroid and adrenal in turn. Preview: gonadal hormones, pancreatic/diabetes pharmacology, and parathyroid disorders continue in Session 2 (Thursday, November 12).

Orient to the arc: the shared HPA-template concept, then three organ systems in turn (pituitary, thyroid, adrenal) that all follow the same hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland logic of Figure 1; Session 2 continues with gonadal hormones, diabetes, and parathyroid disorders on Nov 12.

Readings: Katzung’s Chapters 37–42 are required for Unit 4 (Hypothalamic & Pituitary Hormones; Thyroid & Antithyroid Drugs; Adrenocorticosteroids & Adrenocortical Antagonists; Gonadal Hormones & Inhibitors; Pancreatic Hormones & Glucose-Lowering Drugs; Agents That Affect Bone Mineral Homeostasis).

Session 1 covers Chapters 37–39; Session 2 covers Chapters 40–42. Recommended: Pharmacotherapy Principles and Practice (Chisholm-Burns, Schwinghammer, Malone, Kolesar, Lee, 2022, McGraw-Hill; print ISBN 9781260460278, eText ISBN 9781260460285) as supplemental support, not a substitute.
Required text: Katzung’s Basic and Clinical Pharmacology, 16th Edition (Todd W. Vanderah, 2024/2025, McGraw-Hill Education; ISBN 1260463303 eBook).

**APPENDIX 1** gives **Formulation, dose, indications, adverse effects, contraindications and toxicity** — your study reference: know the dose logic, the one or two serious adverse effects, the contraindication that changes the decision, and the toxicity you would need to recognize.

**Abbreviation key** **PO** **= by mouth** **SC** **= subcutaneous** **IM** **= intramuscular** **IV** **= intravenous** **ER** **= extended-release** **ODT** **= orally disintegrating tablet** **LAR** **= long-acting release** **BID / TID / QID** **= two / three / four times daily** **mcg** **= microgram**

**GH** **= growth hormone** **IGF-1** **= insulin-like growth factor 1** **TSH** **= thyroid-stimulating hormone** **T4 / T3** **= thyroxine / triiodothyronine** **DI** **= diabetes insipidus** **SIADH** **= syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion** **HPA** **= hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal**

**CBC** **= complete blood count** **LFT** **= liver function tests** **QT** **= QT interval on ECG** **CYP** **= cytochrome P450** **MI** **= myocardial infarction** **MRI** **= magnetic resonance imaging** **ARB** **= angiotensin receptor blocker** **AV** **= atrioventricular** **CNS** **= central nervous system**

overview.text: **One regulatory template governs thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal control alike.**

**Figure 1. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): the hypothalamus drives the anterior pituitary, which drives a target endocrine gland, whose peripheral hormone produces end-organ effects and negatively feeds back to suppress the levels above it.**
This is the conceptual spine for the unit — thyroid, adrenal and gonadal pharmacology all map onto this three-level axis; return to it every time a new gland appears.
The peripheral hormone negatively feeds back on the hypothalamus/pituitary above it — which explains why every exogenous hormone therapy in the unit suppresses the levels above it.

prototype.text: Somatropin (GH deficiency); octreotide, lanreotide, pegvisomant (GH excess); cabergoline, bromocriptine (prolactin); desmopressin (DI); tolvaptan, demeclocycline (SIADH).

moa.text: GH axis (Figure 2): pituitary somatotroph releases GH → GH drives liver IGF-1 production → octreotide and lanreotide bind somatostatin receptors and lower GH release.
Pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor so IGF-1 falls → acromegaly symptoms improve (monitor IGF-1). GH rises on pegvisomant, so GH is not used to monitor it.

Dopamine normally inhibits prolactin release — dopamine agonists restore that inhibitory tone. Hypothalamic dopamine is the brake on lactotrophs; prolactinoma or drugs (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) lift the brake.
Cabergoline or bromocriptine activate D2 receptors → prolactin release falls and the tumor often shrinks → cycles and fertility return; galactorrhea resolves.
ADH (Figure 4): ADH binds the V2 receptor in the collecting duct → aquaporin-2 channels insert → water is reabsorbed and urine concentrates.
Desmopressin boosts this (diabetes insipidus); tolvaptan or demeclocycline blunt it (SIADH) → free water retained in DI therapy, excreted in SIADH therapy.
Anterior pituitary hormones & their hypothalamic regulators: continuous (not pulsatile) GnRH analogs down-regulate GnRH receptors and suppress LH and FSH.

indications.text: **●  GH deficiency:** treated with recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin); monitor growth velocity in children and IGF-1 levels in adults.

**●  GH excess (acromegaly):** treated with somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide — suppress GH release), the GH-receptor antagonist pegvisomant, or dopamine agonists (cabergoline) in select cases.
**●  Clinical pearl:** octreotide also has major uses outside the pituitary axis — variceal bleeding and carcinoid syndrome — worth flagging as a cross-system agent.
**●  Indication:** octreotide and lanreotide treat acromegaly; octreotide also treats carcinoid syndrome and variceal bleeding.
Hyperprolactinemia: dopamine agonists are first-line — cabergoline, bromocriptine — used for prolactinomas and drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

Diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency/resistance): desmopressin (DDAVP) for central DI. SIADH (ADH excess): fluid restriction first-line; vasopressin-receptor antagonists (tolvaptan) or demeclocycline for refractory cases.
**●  Somatropin (GH deficiency):** monitor growth velocity or IGF-1.

adverse.text: **●  Adverse effects:** GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia with octreotide and lanreotide (also glucose changes).
**●  Limitation:** pegvisomant does not shrink the tumor; monitor IGF-1 and liver tests.
**●  Adverse effects:** nausea, orthostatic hypotension and dizziness (dopamine agonists).
Cabergoline is twice weekly and better tolerated; high doses link to valvulopathy.
**●  Caution:** high-dose cabergoline in Parkinson patients is linked to cardiac valve fibrosis; use caution with severe psychiatric disease and avoid unmonitored antipsychotic changes.
**●  Desmopressin:** risk is hyponatremia; monitor sodium and limit fluids.
**●  Tolvaptan:** can overcorrect sodium (osmotic demyelination) and cause liver injury; start in hospital.
**●  SIADH:** first-line is fluid restriction; demeclocycline causes photosensitivity and nephrotoxicity.
Short stature from GH deficiency, Turner syndrome and other growth disorders is the main somatropin use; long-acting weekly forms (somapacitan) exist.
Growth hormone (somatropin) adverse effects are rare: pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, scoliosis progression, edema, hyperglycemia.
Mecasermin (recombinant IGF-I for GH-unresponsive growth failure) causes hypoglycemia — give with a carbohydrate meal within 20 minutes.
Octreotide: nausea, cramps, steatorrhea, gallstones, and vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use.

interactions.text: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide raise prolactin by blocking dopamine.

pk.text: **●  Dosing:** cabergoline is better tolerated and given twice weekly; bromocriptine is daily.
Octreotide is 45 times more potent than somatostatin at inhibiting GH; somatostatin analogs come as long-acting monthly depots. Cabergoline’s half-life is about 65 hours.

monitoring.text: **●  Monitoring:** pregnancy testing and prolactin monitoring (dopamine agonists). Monitor IGF-1 for acromegaly therapy.
Pegvisomant does not lower GH secretion and may let the adenoma grow — monitor IGF-I and yearly pituitary MRI.

pearls.text: DI vs. SIADH is a classic exam pairing — opposite problems; anchor it to "which way does free water move" rather than drug names in isolation.
Octreotide reappears in GI/variceal contexts — drug classes are not siloed by organ system.
Hyperprolactinemia causes hypogonadism — infertility, amenorrhea, galactorrhea in women; low libido and ED in men; macroadenomas can compress the optic nerves.
Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) is given IV to start or augment labor; it also triggers milk letdown. Its half-life is about 5 minutes.

overview.text: **Replacing a deficient gland, or slowing down an overactive one.**

**Figure 6. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): iodide trapping, organification, and coupling produce T3/T4, which undergo peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion; methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling, while PTU additionally blocks peripheral conversion.**
Figure 6 is the key to the next slides: PTU, not methimazole, is preferred in thyroid storm because it blocks an extra step.

prototype.text: Levothyroxine (replacement); methimazole, propylthiouracil (thionamides); propranolol; potassium iodide.

moa.text: **Mechanism: synthetic T4, converted peripherally to active T3.**
Levothyroxine path (Figure 5): tablet taken on an empty stomach → absorbed in the small intestine; calcium, iron and antacid binders block it.
T4 converted to active T3 in tissues → T3 binds nuclear receptors and restores metabolism → TSH falls to the target range (recheck at 6–8 weeks).
Methimazole and PTU block organification and coupling; PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion — a faster symptomatic effect in crisis.
Storm targets (Figure 7): Graves thyroid makes excess hormone — PTU blocks synthesis; hormone is released — iodine (after PTU) blocks release.

T4 converts to T3 in tissues — PTU, propranolol and steroids block conversion; T3 stimulates beta receptors — propranolol blunts tachycardia and tremor; crisis settles with fluids, cooling and support.
Thyroid physiology: large doses of iodine inhibit organification (Wolff-Chaikoff block); amiodarone, contrast, β blockers and corticosteroids inhibit T4-to-T3 conversion.

indications.text: Levothyroxine: first-line for hypothyroidism; narrow therapeutic index — dose titrated using TSH (primary hypothyroidism) with repeat labs every 6–8 weeks after a dose change.
About 1.6 mcg/kg/day is full replacement; estrogen raises needs. **●  Pregnancy:** often raises dose needs; monitor TSH closely.
Methimazole: first-line for most non-pregnant patients — once-daily dosing, more convenient; avoid in the first trimester of pregnancy (teratogenic risk).
PTU: preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm. PTU first trimester (lower teratogenic risk) and thyroid storm (also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion).
**A life-threatening hyperthyroid crisis requiring rapid, multi-pronged therapy.** Thyroid storm is treated with four drugs that hit four targets.

Beta-blockers (propranolol) — control adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, tremor) and blunt peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. PTU (preferred over methimazole) — blocks new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion.

Iodine solution (given after PTU/methimazole) — acutely blocks hormone release; must follow the antithyroid drug to avoid providing substrate for new synthesis. Corticosteroids — blunt peripheral conversion and treat relative adrenal insufficiency.

Laboratory diagnosis of Graves disease: suppressed TSH with high free thyroid hormone. Management of Graves disease: antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy; methimazole preferred except in pregnancy and storm.
Pregnant hypothyroid patients often need about 25–30% more levothyroxine; add two extra doses a week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed.

adverse.text: Methimazole boxed warning: agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity. PTU boxed warning: severe hepatotoxicity (more than methimazole) — reserve for specific indications.
Thioamide agranulocytosis occurs in 0.1–0.5%, usually within the first 90 days; PTU’s severe hepatitis (boxed warning) restricts it to the first trimester, thyroid storm, or methimazole reactions.
Both thionamides carry agranulocytosis and liver warnings; PTU has the greater liver risk. Fever or sore throat on a thionamide means stop and check a CBC.
**●  Over-replacement:** tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and bone loss.
Iodides given alone can escape in 2–8 weeks and worsen thyrotoxicosis; avoid chronic iodide in pregnancy (fetal goiter).

contra.text: **Older adults and patients with cardiac disease: start at lower doses and titrate slowly to avoid precipitating angina/arrhythmia.**
**●  Propranolol:** avoided in decompensated heart failure and asthma.
Radioactive iodine (131I) is avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding — it destroys the fetal thyroid.

interactions.text: **Significant absorption interactions: calcium, iron, and antacids can all reduce absorption — separate dosing by at least 4 hours.**
**●  Timing:** separate from calcium, iron, antacids, PPIs and bile acid binders by 4 hours.

Amiodarone and lithium can cause hypo- or hyperthyroidism. Estrogens raise thyroid-binding globulin, so levothyroxine needs rise. Rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine speed clearance of levothyroxine and steroids.
**●  Steroids:** also treat relative adrenal insufficiency; avoid aspirin in thyroid storm (it frees bound hormone).

pk.text: Take on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast, consistently relative to other medications and food.
T4 has a 7-day half-life (allows once-daily dosing); T3 about 1 day. Enzyme inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) speed thyroid hormone metabolism.

monitoring.text: **●  Start low:** in older adults and in cardiac disease. Check TSH at 6–8 weeks.

pearls.text: The absorption-interaction list is extremely high-yield — many patients also take calcium or iron, so timing counseling matters as much as the drug itself.
The pregnancy-trimester switch (PTU in first trimester, methimazole after) is a frequently tested nuance — worth stating explicitly rather than assuming one drug is simply "better."
**●  Sequence:** start PTU and beta-blocker first; give iodine at least an hour later. **●  PTU:** boxed warning for hepatotoxicity.
Case: fever, tachycardia, and altered mental status in untreated Graves disease. **What is the correct sequence of pharmacologic therapy, and why does the order matter?**

**Beta-blockade and PTU are started first; iodine solution is given only after PTU, since giving iodine first would supply additional substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis before the gland’s synthetic machinery is blocked — potentially worsening the crisis.**
Iodine-first sequencing is the classic high-yield detail: giving iodine first can worsen the crisis by supplying substrate before synthesis is blocked.
Subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal hormones) affects 4–10%; amiodarone causes hypo- or hyperthyroidism (about 3% thyrotoxicosis) that persists after stopping.
Subacute thyroiditis releases stored hormone transiently; nontoxic goiter in the US is most often Hashimoto thyroiditis; neonatal Graves comes from maternal antibodies.

overview.text: **Glucocorticoid power and mineralocorticoid balance — and what happens when therapy stops.**

**Figure 9. Original illustrative diagram (not from Katzung): chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses CRH and ACTH via negative feedback, reducing endogenous cortisol production — abrupt withdrawal can precipitate adrenal insufficiency.**
This is the single most clinically important concept in the glucocorticoid section — it explains why tapering (not stopping) is the standard of care.

prototype.text: Prednisone, dexamethasone, hydrocortisone (glucocorticoids); fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid); ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone (antagonists).

moa.text: Glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone, dexamethasone): anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects, with a spectrum of relative potency and mineralocorticoid activity across agents.

Signaling (Figure 8): prednisone or cortisol crosses the cell membrane → binds the cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor → the complex moves into the nucleus → switches on anti-inflammatory genes and represses NF-kB cytokines → fewer inflammatory cells and mediators.
Mineralocorticoids (fludrocortisone): promote renal sodium retention and potassium excretion.

Synthesis chain (Figure 10): cholesterol enters the adrenal cortex → CYP enzymes convert it to cortisol and aldosterone → ketoconazole blocks several enzymes; metyrapone blocks the last cortisol step (11-beta-hydroxylase).
Then cortisol or aldosterone binds its receptor → mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor. Receptor blockers leave hormone levels high.

indications.text: Glucocorticoids are used across nearly every organ system for inflammatory/autoimmune disease.

Fludrocortisone: replacement therapy in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), alongside a glucocorticoid — primary adrenal insufficiency needs BOTH hormone classes replaced, not just cortisol.
**●  Ketoconazole:** inhibits multiple steps in steroidogenesis (CYP enzymes); used for Cushing syndrome; significant drug-interaction and hepatotoxicity concerns.
**●  Metyrapone:** blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis (11-β-hydroxylase); used diagnostically and for Cushing syndrome.

**●  Mifepristone:** a glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperglycemia associated with Cushing syndrome when surgery is not an option (distinct from its progesterone-receptor antagonist use in pregnancy termination).

**●  Spironolactone:** a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist; used for hyperaldosteronism and as a potassium-sparing diuretic — ties back to the diuretic pharmacology concepts from earlier coursework.
Addison disease: hydrocortisone 20–30 mg daily (more during stress) plus fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg/d.
Dexamethasone suppression test diagnoses Cushing syndrome; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce neonatal respiratory distress.

adverse.text: **●  Adverse effects:** hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, infection, mood change, cataracts, adrenal suppression.
**●  Ketoconazole:** hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, strong CYP3A4 inhibition.
**●  Metyrapone:** raises androgens and deoxycorticosterone (hirsutism, hypertension).
**●  Mifepristone:** contraindicated in pregnancy; causes hypokalemia; cortisol levels rise, so monitor clinically. **●  Spironolactone:** hyperkalemia and gynecomastia.
Adrenal suppression can occur after more than 2 weeks of corticosteroids; ACTH does not speed recovery.
Long-term steroids: Cushingoid changes, myopathy, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, masked infection, hypomania or psychosis, posterior subcapsular cataracts.

interactions.text: Azole antifungals raise corticosteroid exposure through CYP3A4. ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium add to spironolactone hyperkalemia. Insulin and oral agents need adjusting during steroid therapy.

pk.text: **●  Potency vs. hydrocortisone:** prednisone about 4x, dexamethasone about 25-30x. **●  Mineralocorticoid action:** fludrocortisone has it; hydrocortisone has both.
**●  Dosing:** take in the morning with food; consider bone and GI protection.
Synthetic corticosteroids — pharmacokinetics & pharmacodynamics: potency and salt-retaining activity differ by agent (equivalent-dose table).
Selection of drug & dosage schedule: give steroids as a single morning dose; alternate-day dosing lessens suppression when disease control allows.

monitoring.text: Fludrocortisone: monitor blood pressure and potassium.
Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis; taper. Chronic suppression leaves the axis unable to resume adequate cortisol quickly — taper, don’t stop abruptly.

pearls.text: Case: chronic high-dose prednisone for a rheumatologic condition, stopped abruptly after running out of refills; now hypotension, weakness, nausea, confusion. **What is the most likely cause of this presentation, and how should it be managed?**
**This presentation is consistent with acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis) from abrupt glucocorticoid withdrawal after HPA-axis suppression.**
**Management requires immediate IV hydrocortisone (which has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity) and IV fluids — this is a medical emergency, not a routine medication-refill issue.**
The fix for a missed refill here is not "just restart the pill" — it is emergent IV steroid replacement; tapering protects against it.

Mifepristone’s dual identity (glucocorticoid-receptor antagonist here vs. progesterone-receptor antagonist elsewhere) is worth flagging explicitly — don’t conflate the two uses or assume a single mechanism.

Drug names reveal the class: **-tide** somatostatin analog (octreotide, lanreotide; lowers GH release); **-pressin** vasopressin analog (desmopressin; central diabetes insipidus); **-vaptan** V2 antagonist (tolvaptan; SIADH).

**-ergoline** dopamine agonist, ergot-derived (cabergoline; lowers prolactin); **-thyroxine** thyroid hormone (levothyroxine; replacement, titrate to TSH); **-imazole / -thiouracil** thionamide antithyroid (methimazole, propylthiouracil; blocks hormone synthesis).

**-sone / -solone** corticosteroid (prednisone, dexamethasone; anti-inflammatory, taper); **-conazole** azole steroidogenesis inhibitor (ketoconazole; Cushing syndrome); **-pristone** receptor antagonist (mifepristone; glucocorticoid-receptor block); **-lactone** mineralocorticoid antagonist (spironolactone; hyperkalemia risk).
**A stem is a memory aid, not a rule: where no shared stem exists, learn the class name instead.**
Recap: **1.** The hypothalamic-pituitary-target gland axis (Figure 1) is a shared regulatory template across thyroid, adrenal, and gonadal systems — drug therapy can intervene at any level.

**2.** Thyroid hormone synthesis has distinct, drug-targetable steps (Figure 6); PTU uniquely blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, making it preferred in thyroid storm and first-trimester pregnancy.
**3.** Chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use suppresses the HPA axis (Figure 9) — abrupt withdrawal risks adrenal crisis, so chronic therapy is tapered, not stopped.

**4.** Adrenocortical antagonists (ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone, spironolactone) block cortisol or aldosterone synthesis/action at different points for Cushing syndrome and hyperaldosteronism. **5.** Session 2 (Thursday, November 12) continues with gonadal hormones, diabetes, and parathyroid disorders.
Older synthesis inhibitors — aminoglutethimide and trilostane — and the adrenolytic mitotane are rarely used; mifepristone (RU-486) is the receptor antagonist.
Synthesis inhibitors & glucocorticoid antagonists: metyrapone is the only adrenal inhibitor usable in pregnancy; abiraterone treats refractory prostate cancer; mifepristone half-life about 20 hours.
